units: the writer is sending a letter to a friend from a shared allotment
the young plants were no longer coming up out of the seed
the surface of the soil had hardened into a tight crust
water slid off towards a drainage channel instead of soaking down to the roots
a grower on the neighbouring plot suggested a tried and tested remedy
the soil material was sieved to take out the stones
an organic amendment was worked in to hold water where it could be used
the surface is broken up after every watering
the plants came through after roughly three weeks
text: Dear friend, I am writing from the shared allotment I described at the start of the season. Nothing was germinating. The seeds simply sat there, and none of us could work out what was holding them back. The topsoil had baked into a tight crust, so the water ran straight across it, escaped down the drainage channel and never reached the roots. The grower on the neighbouring plot put us right; he has relied on the same remedy for years. We sieved the soil to remove the stones, then worked in well rotted compost, which retains moisture without smothering the young shoots. After every watering, somebody goes along the row and breaks the surface up with a hand fork. Three weeks or so later the first leaves pushed through, thick and sturdy. I shall send a picture once the row fills out. Do write and tell me whether your balcony is fruiting.

units: a specialist in insects compares two kinds of pollinator
hived colonies hold a very large body of workers
hived foragers travel long distances
wild species settle on their own in hollow stems or slopes of loose sand
wild species range over a small radius
wild species work flowers that the others pass over
the specialist refuses to name one kind as better
an orchard left to hives alone yields an uneven crop
ground with few flowers defeats both kinds
text: Are wild bees a match for kept bees when it comes to pollination? People ask it constantly, and an entomologist I put the question to answered with a comparison. Hived colonies work in huge numbers, she said, and their foragers will travel a long way before bringing the load home; their strength is sheer weight of workers. Wild species nest on their own, in a hollow stem or a slope of loose sand, they range only a short way, and they work flowers the others pass over; their strength is precision. So which would she pick? Neither, she laughed. An orchard left to hived colonies alone crops unevenly, because part of the blossom opens on cold days, when the hive stays shut. Ground edged with hedges and bare banks gets both services at once. Then she added a caveat: where wild flowers are scarce, neither kind will hold on.

units: the head of a laboratory presents her monitoring beside a body of water
she sets out the markers used to judge a watercourse
the insect larvae living under the stones make up the first marker
the loss of those larvae points to contamination
a spread of algae over the bed betrays fertiliser coming off the farmland
a coloured floating object serves to gauge the speed of the current
the state of the banks is among the markers that get overlooked
a bank stripped of plants gives way as soon as the water rises
bankside shrubs bind the soil and house birds
a proper assessment calls for repeated observation
text: The head of the laboratory meets us beside a shallow pool, a hand lens ready in her palm. She runs through the markers her team records to judge the health of a river. The first, she says, sits under the stones: the insect larvae clinging there cannot cope with loaded water, so if they have gone, something is getting in. The second is the algae carpeting the bed. Where it thickens, fertiliser has seeped down from the fields alongside. The third is the speed of the current, which a coloured float will gauge well enough. She ends on a marker most people overlook, the bank itself. A bare bank collapses the moment the water rises, while a bank thick with shrubs binds the soil and shelters the birds that nest close to the surface. None of this, she says, can be read off in a single visit.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: a worker in glass notices the magnifying effect of a curved piece of glass
clear stones were cut and rubbed smooth so that fine writing could be read
wooden mounts were made to hold the gap between the eye and the lens
those mounts left the hands free
a lens maker set two glasses one above the other inside a cylinder
that stacking pushed the enlargement further still
minute creatures were spotted in stagnant water
the presence of living things in a single droplet astounded the learned
the flaws of colour around the rim were cured as the craft improved
the instrument ended by making the basic unit of life visible
text: Long before science had instruments to its name, a glassworker noticed that a rounded splinter of glass swelled the threads of the cloth beneath it. Curiosity did the rest. Clear stones were cut, then rubbed smooth with sand, so that cramped writing could be read. Wooden mounts followed, holding the lens a fixed distance from the eye and leaving both hands free. A lens grinder thought of setting two glasses one above the other inside a tube, and the image swelled again. A patient watcher found tiny creatures wriggling in a drop of stale water, and the notion that a whole living thing could sit inside a droplet shook the learned world. Later hands polished better and cured the coloured fringes that blurred the rim, until the instrument laid bare the cell. What the naked eye withheld, glass gave up.

units: a dried out seed puts its biological workings on hold
that state lets it withstand extreme conditions
taking up water swells the tissues and splits the protective coat
the arrival of water wakes enzymes
those enzymes turn the stored starch into usable sugars
the root heads downwards under the pull of gravity
the shoot grows the opposite way
mild warmth speeds up the enzyme reaction
excessive heat wrecks the enzymes and halts the emergence
waterlogged soil drives out the oxygen and rots the young plant
text: While a seed stays dry, nothing stirs inside it. Its workings are on hold, and it will come through conditions that would kill a full grown plant. The moment moisture crosses the coat, the tissues swell and the pressure splits the shell open. That inrush of water wakes enzymes, and they cut the stored starch into sugars the plant can draw on. The sugars feed the embryo, which starts into growth: a root drives downwards, pulled by gravity, while a shoot climbs the other way. Warmth hurries the whole business along, since enzymes work faster in a mild medium; past a certain point, though, they break down and the seedling stalls. Too much water does something much like it. It drives the air out of the soil, leaves the tissues without oxygen, and rots the young plant before the first leaf ever shows.

units: a seed keeping station changed its procedure after a technical fault
the smallest seeds were clinging to the metal surfaces of the sorting machine
that clinging built the seeds into clumps
the weight readings were thrown out by it
the worker took an electric shock near the feed hopper
seeds rubbing against dry metal were throwing off static
replacing the equipment was beyond what the site could afford
a technician advised running the metal parts to earth through a conductor
she also called for damping the air in the room
the fault stopped during the following harvest period
text: At a seed store, a trivial mishap ended up rewriting a whole procedure. The technician on the sorting bench noticed that the smallest seeds were clinging to the metal walls of the machine and building into clumps, which threw out every weighing they made. Reaching towards the feed hopper, he took a shock, and a bluish spark jumped across to the panel. Static, thrown off by the husks rubbing against dry steel, accounted for the fault. Management first looked at replacing the plant, an outlay well beyond anything the site could find. An engineer put forward two far plainer measures: run a copper wire from every metal part down to earth, and keep the air of the room moderately damp with a fine spray. The clumps had gone by the following harvest, and the weighings could be trusted again.

units: the kit takes in a clear jar, a mesh sieve, a pouring cone, a pair of tweezers and a magnifying lens
two separate ways serve to draw the living things out of a soil sample
the two ways answer different aims
the way without water is to shake the crumbled earth on the sieve above a pale surface
the mineral grains drop through the mesh
the crawling animals are held back on top
the tweezers serve to move the animals under the lens without harming them
the way with water is to thin the sample down and then let the particles settle
roots and eggs come up to the top while the sand sinks
the first way suits looking at whole insects and the second gauging how much sand there is
text: You will need a clear jar, a fine sieve, a funnel, a soft pair of tweezers and a magnifying lens. There are two ways of separating living things from a sample of soil, and the two of them answer quite different questions. The dry way is to crumble the clod onto the sieve and shake it gently above a sheet of pale paper. Mineral grains drop through the mesh, the crawling animals stay on top, and the tweezers will lift them across under the lens without damaging them. The wet way asks you to fill the jar with water, stir the clod into it, then let everything settle before pouring the cloudy liquid through the funnel. Roots and eggs come to the top, while the sand sinks. Take the first when you want whole insects to look at, the second when you want to gauge how much sand there is.

units: a party of about twenty volunteers goes out after the sun has gone down
their aim is to count the amphibians round a body of water
two volunteers help the toads across a road
another post is netting the animals so that they can be named
the animals caught are put straight back in the water
every sighting is written down with the time and the water temperature
the woman in charge says that readings piled up over several seasons bring out shifts
one set of readings on its own is not enough to bring out those shifts
the woman in charge admits the conditions are rough and sometimes come to nothing
text: There are about twenty of them, boots on and lamps strapped to their foreheads, and they head down to the pond once the light has gone. They are volunteers, and the job comes down to a head count of amphibians. First post, the road: two of them tally the toads crossing and carry them over the bank. Second post, the water's edge: a net goes in, the species is named, the animal goes straight back. Third post, the notebook: every sighting is written down with the time and the water temperature. The coordinator explains that these figures, added up from one season to the next, bring out shifts that no single night could ever show. She owns up to the thankless side of it as well: the cold, the mud, the evenings that turn up nothing. Then a call rises from the ditch, and the whole group stops to listen.

units: the calm look of the surface hides the activity below the water
at the end of the cold season the deposit on the bed gives off bubbles
a greenish layer spreads along the edges
sticky clusters fasten themselves to the drowned plants
the embryos end by coming out of their eggs
the dark larvae gather in crowds near the warmed edge
the larvae feed on the algae coating the stones
the hind limbs form while the tail piece shrinks away
the falling level packs the last larvae into a small stretch of water
the ones that have changed leave the water for the plant cover
text: Nothing on the surface gives away what is being got ready underneath it. As the cold season loosens its hold, the mud lets go of its bubbles and a green film creeps along the edges of the pond. Jelly-like clusters show up between the stems, fastened to the reeds under the water. They pale, they fill with dark commas, and the eggs hatch at last. Black tadpoles swarm in dark clouds near the warm shallows, grazing the algae that coat the stones. Their shape alters without a sound: back legs push out, the tail shrinks away, the skin darkens. When the heat turns heavy, the level falls away, the mud cracks, and the last tadpoles crowd into one narrow puddle. The ones that have changed take to the long grass. The clear water of the season to come will keep no trace at all of any of it.

units: hedgerows are coming out faster than new ones go in
taking those hedgerows out makes it easier for farm machinery to get about
the wind sweeps the opened ground with nothing in its way
the layer of soil that feeds the crop is carried off into the ditches
rainwater tears down the slopes and cuts gullies into them
the watercourses take in more silt
the birds that used to settle in those branches have grown scarce
the drop in those predators drives up the use of sprays against crop pests
replanting is money laid out with nothing to show for it straight away
text: Hedgerows are coming out faster than they go back in, and the bill is already showing in the fields. Every screen of branches taken away makes the ground easier to work with machinery, granted. But the wind, which used to meet something living in its path, now sweeps a bare surface and carries the fertile layer off into the ditches. Storm water does the same: it tears down the slope unhindered, cuts gullies into it, and goes off to load the rivers with silt. The birds that nested in the thickness of the branches have grown scarce, and with them the predators that kept the crop pests down, so more spraying is needed. A saving in labour is paid for in lost soil, in sprays, in ditches to be dredged. Replanting costs money and returns nothing for several seasons. That is exactly why it should start now.
